tabs.title: Argument and Qualification
tabs.description: Examine the claims and their limits.

tabs.title: Reasoned Application
tabs.description: Evaluate how the argument transfers to educational policy.

questions.q: What makes 'never give up' an inadequate message in some educational settings?
choices: It assumes all pupils will respond to public praise.
It may overlook material obstacles that encouragement cannot remove.
It suggests that students need to set measurable targets.
It treats failure as evidence of an ineffective strategy.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one contrasts motivational slogans with a lack of practical support.

questions.q: What is the significance of the two students receiving similarly poor results?
choices: It proves that their home environments have no effect on learning.
It shows that one student has less determination than the other.
It suggests that assessments cannot identify weaknesses.
It highlights how identical outcomes can conceal unequal opportunities.
questions.explanation: The example deliberately holds performance constant while comparing unequal conditions.

questions.q: How does the discussion of leisure extend the earlier criticism?
choices: It questions the assumption that every valuable activity must show progress.
It shows that schools should measure informal learning more often.
It identifies relaxation as the most reliable way to improve grades.
It argues that studying for pleasure is less useful than formal work.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three broadens the critique to non-measurable forms of learning and curiosity.

questions.q: What would be misleading about praising only the first student's determination?
choices: The student might begin to expect better marks.
The teacher would be unable to compare future work.
The praise might mistake access to resources for personal character.
The other student would no longer benefit from study strategies.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly warns that resource advantages can be confused with strength of character.

questions.q: Which claim is most consistent with the author's view of educational value?
choices: Every learning activity should eventually be converted into a grade.
An experience may be valuable without producing a measurable result.
Leisure becomes valuable only when it leads to a new qualification.
Disagreement is unproductive unless the participants reach consensus.
questions.explanation: Novel reading and thoughtful disagreement are valuable although they may produce no measurable outcome.

questions.q: Why does the final paragraph retain the idea of individual responsibility?
choices: To argue that support should be withdrawn once pupils make progress.
To make students solely responsible for their future opportunities.
To suggest that schools should intervene only when grades fall.
To show that institutional support should enable rather than replace agency.
questions.explanation: The writer states that practical support makes learners' choices more meaningful without removing responsibility.

questions.q: A school puts motivational posters in every corridor but removes supervised study rooms. How would the author most likely respond?
choices: Encouragement without access to practical support leaves the underlying problem unsolved.
The posters would be sufficient if students agreed to work harder.
The change would help students become more independent of teachers.
There is no evidence that study spaces affect students' opportunities.
questions.explanation: The first, second and final paragraphs explicitly distinguish motivation from the resources that make action possible.

questions.q: What concern might the author raise about a school that grades students' hobbies?
choices: The grades could be more reliable than academic assessment.
Students might become unwilling to practise unfamiliar skills.
Activities done for curiosity could become another obligation to improve.
Students might be encouraged to spend more time outside school.
questions.explanation: The author warns that treating leisure as self-optimisation can turn curiosity into a demand.

questions.q: A teacher recommends the same study strategy to every student. What important question is missing?
choices: Whether the teacher has explained the strategy clearly enough.
Whether students actually have the time and conditions to use it.
Whether the strategy can improve marks within a single week.
Whether students already enjoy the subject being taught.
questions.explanation: The comparison between the two students shows that access to time and support changes what advice can achieve.

questions.q: Which policy would best represent the article's overall position?
choices: Replace personal targets with uniform school-wide expectations.
Judge progress exclusively by measurable improvement in grades.
Require students to explain every period of rest or leisure.
Combine specific learning feedback with accessible support and time to rest.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly links personal strategy, institutional support, assessment and rest.
